newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Kinshasa enjoys soft landing for all but a few.
newsitem.headline: Kinshasa enjoys soft landing for all but a few.

text.p: Kinshasa avoided the terrifying bloodbath many had dreaded when Laurent Kabila's rebels walked in almost unopposed.
The city got the soft landing everyone prayed for.
Sunday -- Day Two in the first year of the new Democratic Republic of Congo -- was clean-up day.
There was widespread looting and probably dozens killed before Kabila's rebels consolidated their hold over the city of five million people which they entered on Saturday.
Police and local government buildings were trashed and the rich fled to the safety of hotels.
But compared to other recent upheavals in Central Africa the fall of the Mobutu regime was a smooth operation.

Embassies eased back the bolts on their steel security doors and across the Zaire River in Brazzaville Western commandos who were ready for a Saigon-style evacuation of foreign nationals were told to stand easy.
The charred corpses of six Zaire army soliders who made the mistake of failing to surrender lay among a crowd of curious onlookers on one main boulevard, awaiting pickup by the Red Cross.
A white rib-cage and some shreds of carbonised flesh was all that was left of one of the bodies, burned by a mob.
A few streets away, neatly arranged in a row under a tree, were another five corpses wrapped in grey blankets.
Overloaded cars, pickup trucks and minibuses, all sporting the white rag that denotes backing for the revolution, slowed down to let passengers take a look.

At army barracks across the city, former Zaire soldiers, gendarmes, police and civil guards were coming in with their weapons and their hands up, obeying the rebel Alliance's broadcast order to surrender by Sunday night.
Hundreds of automatic rifles were piled up bonfire fashion at Camp Mobutu barracks, and a long line of men now in civilian clothes waited to register with the new military authorities.
A rebel sergeant handed out the best of the regular army's lightweight raincoats to Kabila's modestly equipped troops.
"This is liberation," he said, to no-one in particular. "We will take everything."

On the wide Boulevard of June 30, named for independence day in 1960, a long column of Kabila soldiers deployed with their inimitable mix of indolence and menace. They don't march as much as slouch, with a bored, dont-mess-with-me air.
Some carried bedding on their heads and others cradled light machineguns wreathed in tangles of brass-bulleted ammunition belt. An entourage of frond-waving admirers followed their slow deployment.
In Kitambo, a poor district where shops and bars had been smashed and looted, the dense crowd which swarmed upon a carload of touring reporters seemed near hysteria.
But on the newly renamed Voice of Congo radio, an orderly tone of bright optimism and moral righteousness prevailed.
An announcer read out the descriptions and registration numbers of stolen cars that were to be returned.

"The level of looting has gone beyond the bounds of the tolerable," he said, unconsciously acknowledging that the sacking of shops was something to be taken into normal account in a country where the gap between rich and poor is obscene.
"Certain workers have had no pay since certain company managers have run off with the money," the radio observed.
